newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM urges independent probe of grenade blast.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM urges independent probe of grenade blast.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Wednesday called for an independent investigation of a deadly weekend grenade attack, saying he did not trust an interior ministry probe.

Ranariddh, speaking to reporters after visiting the injured in Phnom Penh's Calmette Hospital, put the official toll from Sunday's attack on an opposition protest outside parliament at 19 dead, including two children, and 119 injured.
Co-premiers Hun Sen and Ranariddh agreed on Sunday to set up a joint interior ministry committee to investigate the attack, which both men condemned.

Others have said from 14 to 20 people died in the attack on a demonstration against the judiciary's lack of independence led by opposition Khmer Nation Party leader and apparent target Sam Rainsy, who narrowly escaped injury.

"I think there should be set up a politically neutral committee to investigate this unacceptable crime," Ranariddh said after handing out medicine, food and money to injured in the hospital wards and corridors.

The first prime minister noted that an interior ministry investigation had been launched, "but we should think of the possibility...to try and find out the formula for an independent and politically neutral committee."
Ranariddh and Hun Sen of the Cambodian People's Party (CPP), which rules the country in uneasy coalition with the prince's royalist FUNCINPEC party, agreed on Sunday to let the ministry investigate.

"As prime minister, I have to let the committee do its job but as a Cambodian citizen I don't trust (it)," Ranariddh said. He said the independent body should be made up of Cambodians, but did not elaborate.
Analysts said the authorities had failed to bring to justice those behind other incidents of politically motivated violence since the coalition was formed after U.N.-run polls in 1993.
Sam Rainsy, at a sombre cremation service for victims on Wednesday, vowed to continue fighting for democracy and human rights despite Sunday's violence.

"Other people -- many other people -- are prepared to sacrifice their lives until justice prevails in Cambodia," he told mourners, including distraught family members and diplomats from the United States, Australia, Japan and Canada.
Sam Rainsy, who has blamed his bitter enemy co-Premier Hun Sen for the attack, said he hoped Hun Sen would "stop causing terrible suffering to innocent people".
Ranariddh said the tragedy was a major setback for democracy in Cambodia and reiterated: "It was not an isolated incident. I think it was a very well planned assassination attempt."

He told Reuters on Tuesday he feared the attack marked the onset of further violence ahead of coming elections in 1998 and doubted whether polls could be free and fair without a strong presence of international observers.

Ranariddh and Hun Sen's political parties are expected to oppose each other in the next elections, and Ranariddh said it would become "more and more difficult" for the two leaders to work together as the polls approached.
In a sign that fears of attack remain acute, security appeared tight at Wednesday's funeral services at Wat Langka, where five bodies were being cremated.
A guard dressed in black patted down each mourner for weapons, and armed police stood in front of the temple gates.
Mourners had set up a makeshift shrine with flowers, wreaths and a banyan tree at the scene of the blast, but they were removed by garbage men shortly after noon.
